Napoleon conquered armies, defeated kings, and nearly took over Europe.
But one day, he was forced to retreat from a battlefield...
because of a thousand rabbits.
Give me 60 seconds, and I'll show you how the most feared military commander in Europe got bullied by fluffy little animals.
It was 1807.
Napoleon had just celebrated a major diplomatic victory, and his chief of staff, Alexandre Berthier, wanted to organize something special.
A rabbit hunt.
He ordered around 1,000 rabbits to be brought to a nearby hunting ground.
Sounds simple, right?
Well, Berthier made one tiny mistake.
He bought domesticated rabbits instead of wild ones.
And when the cages opened, Napoleon expected the rabbits to run away.
But they did the exact opposite.
Instead of escaping, the rabbits charged straight toward him.
Why?
Because these weren't wild animals.
They were used to being fed by humans.
And apparently, an entire army of rabbits had just mistaken Napoleon for the guy delivering lunch.
His men tried chasing them away with sticks and whips.
But the rabbits kept coming.
They surrounded the hunters, swarmed around Napoleon's legs, and even followed him toward his carriage.
Eventually, the emperor had enough.
The man who had faced entire European armies was retreating from a bunch of hungry bunnies.
Now, there's a catch:
this story comes mainly from a general's memoirs published decades later,
so historians can't confirm every detail.
But if it happened anything like the account describes,
Napoleon's most embarrassing opponent wasn't Britain, Russia, or Austria.
It was lunch.
